The Story of Yampal the Chandala

I bow to Lord Jina, the bestower of liberation, and I write the story of a chandala whom even the gods worshipped.

King Pakshashasan of Kashi, seeing his people afflicted by a great plague, had a proclamation beaten through the city: "No creature shall be killed for eight days during the Nandishvar festival. Whoever violates this royal decree shall be sentenced to death." In that city lived a merchant's son named Dharma — though in truth he was utterly adharmic. He was addicted to seven vices and had a terrible habit of eating meat. He could not pass a single day without it.

One day he went secretly to the king's garden. There stood the king's prized ram, and Dharma killed it, ate its raw flesh, and buried the bones in a pit. Truly it is said: "A person addicted to vices is always engaged in sin."

The next day, when the king found the ram missing and all searches failed, he appointed many spies. One spy went to the royal garden, where the gardener was telling his wife at night about the merchant's son killing the ram. The spy overheard everything and reported it to the king. The king was furious and ordered the kotwal to take the wicked Dharma and hang him on the gallows, for he had committed both violence against a living being and violated the royal decree.

The kotwal led Dharma to the execution ground and sent servants to summon Yampal the chandala, whose duty it was to carry out executions. But Yampal had once heard the sacred teaching of Jain dharma from a monk endowed with the power of all medicinal herbs, and had taken a vow: "I shall never kill any living being on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight." Seeing the royal servants approaching, and knowing it was Chaturdashi, he said to his wife to protect his vow — "Beloved, the king's men are coming to call me to kill someone. I must hide, for today is Chaturdashi and I cannot break my vow."

He went into hiding, and the servants could not find him. They returned and told the kotwal, who then ordered Dharma to be executed by someone else. But before the execution could take place, a remarkable thing happened. Dharma, standing at the gallows, remembered the teachings he had once casually heard from a Jain monk. In that moment of mortal terror, he sincerely repented for all his sins and recited the Namaskar Mantra with genuine devotion.

The execution was carried out, but Dharma's sincere repentance at the moment of death, combined with the merit of the Namaskar Mantra, transformed his destiny. He was reborn in a heavenly realm. Meanwhile, Yampal the chandala, through his steadfast observance of his vow of non-violence on sacred days, accumulated great merit and eventually attained a higher birth and spiritual progress.

This story teaches two great lessons. First, that sacred vows protect even those of the lowest birth — Yampal the chandala, through his vow, earned the worship of the gods. Second, that sincere repentance, even at the last moment, can redeem the most wicked soul. No one is beyond the reach of grace, and no vow, however small, goes unrewarded.
